vignette:
Nadia is a 27-year-old animator who lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment in Los Angeles. She came to therapy six months after the end of a relationship with a man named Carlos, whom she had been seeing for nearly two years. The physical abuse began about a year in, starting with what she described as "rough play" that sometimes left bruises, then escalated into incidents where he would grab her by the wrists, shake her, or push her into walls during arguments. The worst episode happened on a rainy Tuesday night in December. She had come home late from a deadline at the studio, and Carlos accused her of lying about where she had been. When she tried to walk past him to the bathroom, he grabbed her by the hair and slammed her head against the doorframe. She remembered the sound more than the pain—a hollow crack that seemed to come from inside her skull. After that night, she stopped fighting back. She would go still and quiet when he was angry, hoping that if she didn't move or speak, he would stop sooner. That stillness, that silence, is what haunts her now more than the bruises.

Nadia believes she has permanently changed for the worse. She told her intake clinician that she feels like a different person now—someone who is smaller, more cautious, less sure of herself. She used to be the kind of person who would speak up in meetings, who would pitch wild ideas for animated sequences, who would laugh loudly at her own jokes. Now she sits at her desk with headphones on, working on the same shot for hours because she cannot stop second-guessing her choices. She is certain that the event happened because of the way she acted—specifically, because she did not leave him sooner, because she made excuses for him, because she kept coming home. She replays those months in her mind and sees only her own failures: the texts she did not send to friends, the times she deleted voicemails from her mother asking if she was okay, the morning after the doorframe incident when she went to work and said nothing. She also feels that she acted in ways that go against who she is. The woman who went still and silent, who learned to make herself small and compliant, is not the woman she recognizes. She told her therapist, "I stayed. I let him do that to me. That's not who I am, but I did it anyway." She cannot reconcile the person she was before with the person she became in that apartment, and that fracture feels like a kind of moral injury she carries alone.

At work, Nadia avoids any scene that involves a character being grabbed or shaken. She has started asking her supervisor to reassign those shots to other animators, claiming she is better at facial expressions than action sequences. She has also stopped going to the studio's weekly happy hours, because she cannot stand the sound of raised voices in a crowded room—it makes her chest tighten and her vision blur. She has told no one at work about Carlos. She is afraid that if they knew, they would see her the way she sees herself: weak, foolish, permanently damaged. She has come to therapy because she is exhausted by the constant self-blame and by the feeling that she is living in a body and a life that no longer belong to her. She is most afraid that she will never feel like herself again.
